The Best Motorcycle Roads in the Lake District: A Rider's Complete Guide

I've been touring the Lake District on two wheels for over a decade, and I can tell you there's nowhere quite like it in Britain for motorcycle touring. The combination of challenging mountain passes, stunning lakeside routes, and proper riding roads makes this corner of Cumbria absolutely essential for any serious tourer. After countless trips through these fells, I've put together what I reckon are the absolute best roads for getting the most out of your Lake District adventure.

The Lakes offer everything from gentle cruise routes perfect for pillion passengers to proper mountain passes that'll test your skills and your bike. I've ridden every road mentioned here in all conditions – sunshine, torrential rain, and that peculiar Lakes mist that can roll in without warning. Here's what you need to know to make the most of your trip.

Essential Lake District Motorcycle Routes

Kirkstone Pass (A592): The Classic Challenge

Starting with the big one – Kirkstone Pass remains my go-to recommendation for anyone wanting to experience proper Lake District riding. This 1,489-foot pass between Ambleside and Patterdale is the highest road pass in the Lakes, and you'll feel every foot of that elevation gain.

The approach from Ambleside is relentless – a steady climb with hairpins that tighten as you gain height. Your bike will work for this one, especially if you're two-up with touring kit. I always drop down a gear earlier than I think I need to; the gradient catches out plenty of riders who find themselves lugging the engine halfway up.

The descent into Patterdale on the eastern side is where the real fun begins. The road opens up with sweeping bends that flow beautifully, giving you proper views across to Helvellyn. Just watch for sheep – they've got absolutely no road sense and will wander into your line without warning.

Weather warning: Kirkstone Pass can be properly grim in the wet. I've been caught in cloud up there where visibility dropped to about 20 metres. If the weather's closing in, there's no shame in turning back – the pass will still be there tomorrow.

Honister Pass (B5289): Technical Riding at Its Best

This is my favourite technical road in the Lakes. The B5289 from Borrowdale to Buttermere via Honister Pass is only about 6 miles long, but what a 6 miles. The western approach from Borrowdale starts gentle enough, following Honister Beck through some lovely woodland sections.

Then it gets serious. The road ramps up through a series of tight hairpins carved into the fellside. These aren't flowing bends – they're proper 180-degree switchbacks that demand respect. I've seen plenty of riders get caught out by the tightening radius on some of these corners. Take them steady the first time through.

The summit section runs past the old slate mine workings – it's like riding through an industrial moonscape. Fascinating stuff, but keep your eyes on the road. The descent towards Buttermere is sublime – fast, flowing curves with Buttermere and Crummock Water spread out below you.

Top tip: There's often loose slate debris on this road, especially after rain. It's like riding on marbles, so adjust your cornering accordingly.

Hardknott and Wrynose Passes: The Double Challenge

Right, this is where we separate the committed tourers from the Sunday riders. The combination of Hardknott Pass (30% gradient) and Wrynose Pass makes for one of the most challenging motorcycle routes in England. I won't lie – these roads will test you and your machine.

Starting from the west, the approach to Hardknott from Eskdale is deceptive. It starts as a pleasant cruise through the valley, then hits you with gradients that would make a mountain goat think twice. I've seen cars rolling backwards here, and motorcycles struggling with clutch slip.

The key is momentum and the right gear. I always approach in second gear and resist the urge to change down further – you need the torque delivery to be smooth and predictable. If your bike starts struggling, there are a couple of spots where you can pull over safely, but they're limited.

Wrynose Pass follows immediately after, and by this point, your clutch hand will be getting a proper workout. The road's narrower here, with some blind summits that require real caution. But the sense of achievement when you complete both passes is immense.

Essential gear check: Make sure your bike's cooling system is in top condition before attempting these passes. I've seen overheating issues on hot days, particularly with air-cooled machines working hard at low speeds.

Scenic Lakeside Routes

Ullswater Circuit (A592 and A5091): Perfect for Pillions

When I want to show someone why the Lakes are special without scaring them senseless, this is where I take them. The circuit around Ullswater combines proper riding roads with scenery that'll have you stopping every few miles for photos.

Starting from Pooley Bridge, the A5091 runs along the western shore through some lovely wooded sections. The road surface is generally excellent, and the curves are gentle enough to maintain a good pace while still enjoying the views. Howtown is a perfect coffee stop – there's good parking for bikes and the café does proper bacon sandwiches.

The A592 return leg along the eastern shore is more open, with long sweeping bends and better overtaking opportunities. The views across the lake towards Helvellyn are spectacular, especially in late afternoon light. Just watch for tourists in rental cars moving at glacial pace – patience is a virtue on Lake District roads.

Coniston Water and the Old Man

The A593 around Coniston Water offers a different character entirely. It's less about technical riding and more about soaking up the atmosphere. The eastern shore road has some lovely sections through mature woodland, with glimpses of the lake between the trees.

The real treat is the minor road that branches off towards the Old Man of Coniston. It climbs steadily through increasingly dramatic scenery before eventually becoming unsuitable for road bikes. But the riding section gives you a taste of proper Lake District solitude – on a weekday, you might not see another vehicle for miles.

Hidden Gems and Lesser-Known Routes

The Langdale Valley Road

This is one of those roads that doesn't appear on many touring lists, but it absolutely should. The B5343 from Ambleside to the head of Great Langdale is a proper rider's road disguised as a tourist route.

The initial section through Elterwater is gentle enough, but as you head deeper into the valley, the road becomes more challenging. There are some lovely fast sections with well-sighted bends, and the backdrop of the Langdale Pikes is genuinely stunning.

The road ends at the Old Dungeon Ghyll Hotel, which has been serving walkers and bikers for decades. The car park can get busy, but there's usually space for bikes, and the beer garden has brilliant views up towards Pike of Blisco.

Thirlmere Circuit

Here's a route that many riders miss entirely, which is their loss. The circuit around Thirlmere combines good riding with relative peace and quiet – it's the anti-Windermere, if you like.

The western shore road (A591) is the faster option, with some cracking sections where you can make proper progress. The eastern shore follows a minor road that's much more intimate – narrow, twisty, and demanding your full attention. It's like a practice session for the more challenging passes.

The Lake District rewards riders who take time to explore beyond the obvious routes. Some of my best riding memories come from minor roads that barely register on most touring maps.

Practical Considerations for Lake District Touring

Weather and Road Conditions

Let's be honest about Lake District weather – it's unpredictable at best and potentially dangerous at worst. I've started rides in blazing sunshine and finished them in torrential rain. The key is being prepared for everything.

Waterproofs are non-negotiable. I don't care if the forecast shows wall-to-wall sunshine – pack proper wet weather gear. I've been caught out too many times to risk it now. Quality kit from suppliers like SportsBikeShop makes all the difference when the weather turns.

Road surfaces can change dramatically with conditions. That perfect piece of tarmac you enjoyed in the dry becomes treacherous when wet leaves mix with morning dew. The major passes can have ice patches well into spring – I've encountered frost on Kirkstone Pass in late April.

Fuel and Facilities

Petrol stations are scarcer than you might expect, especially once you're deep in the valleys. I always fill up in Ambleside, Keswick, or Kendal before heading into the more remote areas. There's nothing worse than watching your fuel light come on halfway up Hardknott Pass.

Most of the traditional biker cafés are still going strong. The Yan at Kirkstone Pass Inn has been feeding hungry bikers for years, and the portions are generous enough to fuel the next mountain pass. Just be prepared for crowds on summer weekends – arrival before 10am or after 3pm usually guarantees a table.

Traffic and Timing

Summer weekends in the Lakes are genuinely hellish for motorcycle touring. I've learned to avoid them entirely unless absolutely necessary. The combination of holiday traffic, campervans, and inexperienced drivers on challenging roads creates a perfect storm of frustration.

Early morning rides are magical – you'll have many roads virtually to yourself, and the light on the fells is spectacular. Late autumn through early spring offers the best riding conditions, though you'll need to watch the weather more carefully.

Planning Your Lake District Motorcycle Tour

A proper Lake District motorcycle tour needs more planning than your average touring route. The roads are demanding, distances can be deceptive, and facilities are limited in some areas. I always use our trip planning tool to work out realistic daily mileages – what looks like 50 easy miles on the map can take half a day when you factor in the mountain passes and inevitable photo stops.

Accommodation fills up quickly, especially during peak season. B&Bs that welcome motorcyclists and offer secure parking are worth their weight in gold. Book early, and always confirm parking arrangements when you reserve.

For route planning, I recommend breaking the Lakes down into day-long circuits rather than trying to cover everything in one go. A typical day might combine one major pass with some lakeside cruising and time for proper stops. Rushing through the Lakes defeats the entire purpose – this is scenery that demands to be savoured.

Check our packing checklist for mountain touring essentials – the weather can change rapidly at altitude, and being properly prepared makes all the difference between a great day and a survival exercise.

Connecting Routes and Extended Tours

The Lakes work brilliantly as part of longer touring routes. I often combine a Lake District tour with Scotland – our Islands to Highlands route shows how to link the two regions effectively. The A6 north towards Scotland passes through some lovely countryside, and you can be on the Southern Uplands within a couple of hours.

For those planning something more ambitious, the Lakes make an excellent starting point for the NC500 complete route. The riding skills you'll develop on Hardknott and Honister will serve you well on the single-track roads of the Scottish Highlands.

Making the Most of Your Visit

The Lake District isn't just about the riding – though the riding is spectacular. Take time to explore on foot as well. Many of the best viewpoints aren't visible from road level, and a short walk can reveal perspectives that'll make you see familiar roads in an entirely new light.

Local knowledge is invaluable. Strike up conversations with other bikers at cafés and fuel stops – you'll often discover routes and viewpoints that don't appear in any guidebook. The Lake District biking community is welcoming and generous with advice.

Consider the seasons carefully. Spring offers fresh colours and generally good road conditions, though weather can be changeable. Summer brings the best weather but also the crowds. Autumn is my personal favourite – fewer tourists, spectacular colours, and often the most stable weather. Winter riding is possible but demands serious preparation and flexible planning.

Your Next Steps

The Lake District offers some of the finest motorcycle touring in Britain, but it demands respect and preparation. Start with the easier routes like the Ullswater circuit to get a feel for Lakes riding, then progress to the mountain passes as your confidence builds. Use our route builder to plan your itinerary, allowing plenty of time for the unexpected – because in the Lakes, the unexpected is often the highlight of your trip.

Most importantly, ride within your limits and be prepared for changing conditions. The Lakes will still be here next time, and it's better to return safely with stories of great riding than to push beyond your abilities on unfamiliar roads. Pack your wet weather gear, fill your tank, and prepare for some of the most memorable motorcycle touring Britain has to offer. keyTakeaways: The Lakes pack challenging passes and gentle lakeside routes into one compact national park.
Kirkstone Pass (A592) at 1,489 feet is the highest road pass in the Lakes and a classic climb from Ambleside.
Honister Pass (B5289) is the standout technical road, with tight switchbacks and loose slate after rain.
Hardknott and Wrynose (30% gradients) are England's toughest, requiring momentum and cooling-system checks.
The Ullswater circuit is the gentle, pillion-friendly option; ride early and avoid summer weekends.

faq.q: Which is the best all-round Lakes road?
faq.a: Kirkstone Pass, the A592, is the go-to recommendation. At 1,489 feet it is the highest road pass in the Lakes, climbing relentlessly from Ambleside through tightening hairpins before opening into sweeping bends on the descent to Patterdale, with views to Helvellyn. Drop a gear earlier than you think you need to, and watch for sheep with no road sense.

faq.q: What is the most technical road?
faq.a: Honister Pass, the B5289 from Borrowdale to Buttermere, is the finest technical road in the Lakes. It is only about six miles but ramps up through 180-degree switchbacks carved into the fellside past the old slate mine. Beware loose slate debris after rain, which is like riding on marbles, and take the tightening corners steady on your first run.

faq.q: How hard are Hardknott and Wrynose?
faq.a: They are the most challenging passes in England, with gradients touching 30%. Approach Hardknott from Eskdale in second gear and resist changing down further, keeping the torque smooth. Cars have been seen rolling backwards here. Check your cooling system beforehand, as air-cooled engines can overheat working hard at low speed, and expect a real clutch-hand workout on Wrynose.

The Ullswater circuit, using the A592 and A5091, is perfect for pillions. From Pooley Bridge the A5091 runs along the western shore through woodland, with Howtown a fine coffee stop, while the A592 return along the eastern shore offers open sweeping bends and spectacular lake views towards Helvellyn, especially in late-afternoon light.

faq.q: When should I ride the Lakes?
faq.a: Avoid summer weekends, which are genuinely hellish with holiday traffic, campervans and inexperienced drivers on challenging roads. Early morning rides are magical, with quiet roads and superb light on the fells. Autumn is a favourite for fewer tourists and stable weather. Always carry proper waterproofs and fill up in Ambleside, Keswick or Kendal, as fuel is scarce in the fells.
